meta.title: Bulgarian C1 Advanced
meta.subtitle: 1500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Bulgarian → English (see the Bulgarian, recall the meaning) and English → Bulgarian (see an English meaning, recall the Bulgarian). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1500 words for an advanced learner, aligned to C1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand a wide range of demanding, longer texts, and recognise implicit meaning' — a learner here is able to express ideas fluently and spontaneously without much obvious searching for expressions, to use language flexibly and effectively for social, academic and professional purposes, and to produce clear, well-structured, detailed text on complex subjects. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no graded Bulgarian word list is published that a deck could take whole, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 159 of the 1500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — politics, power and the state, law and justice, the economy and finance, science and research, philosophy and belief, language, literature and style, the arts and taste, the mind, emotion and behaviour, society and how it changes, the land and the planet, the small words of nuance, and the verbs of arguing, deciding and shading a meaning — and the other 1341 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Bulgarian, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a noun or a verb added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Every headword is printed in Cyrillic with its stress marked (кни́га, чета́), because Bulgarian stress can fall on any syllable and move as the word changes (град, градове́), and nothing else shows it; there is no transliteration, and the Bulgarian Alphabet deck, the first in this collection, teaches the letters. A verb is given in its first person singular present, the form a Bulgarian dictionary lists (чета́ 'I read', glossed 'to read'), since Bulgarian has no infinitive. The 891 nouns show their gender, their definite form (Bulgarian puts 'the' on the end of the word: кни́гата), their plural and, where it differs, the form used after a number; the 292 verbs show their aspect, imperfective or perfective, with the other verb of the pair beside them, their ти form and their past; and behind the All forms fold every noun's forms and every verb's present, past tenses and imperative by person, with the personal pronouns' full and short forms. Real example sentences come with 375 of the 1500 words, three apiece for 83 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender, aspect, stress and forms: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
